source.title: Minimum Operations to Halve Array Sum

teaching.hint: What reduction does halving one current value buy, and how does that value change before it can be chosen again?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Each element offers a descending sequence of possible reductions: half its original value, then a quarter, and so on. Choosing the largest available reduction collects the best possible total after any fixed number of moves.
solution_outline.approach: Keep current values in a maximum-priority structure. Repeatedly halve the largest current value, add that half to the total reduction, and put the halved value back. Stop when the reduction reaches at least half the original sum.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The structure contains exactly the current value of every element. After t moves, the reduction is the sum of the t largest feasible marginal gains across their decreasing per-element chains.
solution_outline.correctness: An element's later gain cannot exceed its earlier gain, so the largest uncollected gain is always available as the next halving of some current element. Greedy therefore maximizes reduction for every operation count t. The first t meeting the required threshold is the minimum possible count.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space: at most n operations are needed because halving every element once already reaches half the original sum. Exact-threshold arithmetic needs care with fractional halves.
solution_outline.pitfall: Stopping only when the reduction is strictly greater than half adds an operation when equality already satisfies the goal; repeated floating rounding can obscure that boundary.

common_wrong_turns: Sort once and never reconsider a halved element
Discard a value after halving it once
Use a strict greater-than test at the target
source_fidelity_notes: Long operation traces were omitted; fractional repeated halving, original-sum threshold, at-least equality, and input bounds were retained.
